notes: Summary: Obsidian is evaluating Redwood Dedicated + Private for a latency-sensitive trading-assist app. Primary ask: rigorous alignment on SLO definitions and measurement points before committing reserved GPUs.
Observed problem: internal metrics team reports server-side token generation timing while frontend product counts full client perceived time — mismatch leads to divergent p99 values.

SLO proposal discussed: define application SLOs in two layers — Infra SLO (server-side generation, per-request compute time) and End-to-end SLO (client-side end-to-end, includes network + streaming). Both tracked but only E2E used for customer-facing SLA.

Percentiles: agreed baseline p50/p95/p99 buckets. Clarify calculation method: use sliding-window 5m aggregation, then compute quantiles from raw latencies (not quantile-approx summaries) for SLA reporting. Keep histogram snapshots every 1m for auditability.

Streaming vs non-streaming: streaming requests to be measured per-"first-token-latency" and also per-completion-latency. Non-streaming (batch) measured by request completion time. SLOs: streaming p95-first-token <= 80ms, streaming p95-completion <= 250ms for 1-2k token responses (target workload).

Client-side timing: instrument frontends with synthetic trace id forwarded to backend. Use distributed tracing (trace id in request header) so server logs can correlate client-perceived latency. For SLA, use client-collected traces as authoritative E2E dataset; server metrics used for root-cause and billing reconciliation.

Sampling & noise: sample 100% of failed/error requests for post-mortem; sample 10% of successful requests for full traces. For SLA calc, extend sample weighting to approximate full set; discuss extrapolation methodology with Obsidian analytics.

Warm vs cold cache: define separate operational windows — warming window (first 10 minutes after deploy) excluded from SLA; cold-start p99 tracked but not penalized. KV/prefix cache hits to be surfaced in dashboards; recommend baseline cache warmers during rollouts.

Throughput guarantees: Redwood to propose GPU reservation plan: baseline reserved GPUs to sustain 500 concurrent conversational sessions (avg 2 tokens/sec/session) with 5% headroom. Autoscaling burst allowed up to 2x for 24h/month. Must tie to cost and contractual terms.

Batching & concurrency: production throughput optimized via continuous batching. Service-side concurrency cap per-GPU and per-model will be defined. Obsidian wants explicit concurrency SLAs (max queue latency contribution) — AE to include in term sheet.

SLA penalties: negotiation point — Obsidian prefers crediting model: 10% monthly credits if E2E p99 > contractual threshold for 3 days in month. Redwood legal flagged operational complexity; proposed pilot metric period before hard SLA.

Measurement alignment items for next doc: exact percentile algorithm (t-digest vs exact), windowing/aggregation, excluded events list (deployments/maintenance), definition of first-byte vs last-byte for streaming, and canonical trace header format.
Quote from Head of Platform (Obsidian): 'We can't buy reserved GPUs until we can measure the thing we pay for — need a rock-solid, auditable p99 that maps to customer experience.'

Actionable recommendations given to customer: 1) agree on canonical trace header, 2) run 1-week shadow run with production traffic, 3) produce side-by-side dashboard (client vs server percentiles) and reconciled SLA report, 4) finalize reserve sizing after shadow run results.
